Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Overeating: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Vignette:
Tan Nguyen still wakes up every morning at 5 am, just like he did when his wife, Linh, was alive. But now, instead of getting dressed for another day as a public defender, he lies in bed and listens to the sounds of the city outside their apartment window. He's waiting for the noises that will convince him it's safe to get up – the distant hum of traffic, the chatter of pedestrians on the sidewalk below. Only when he's satisfied that all is quiet does he throw off the covers and begin his daily routine. It's been three years since Linh was mugged and killed outside their favorite Vietnamese restaurant in Chinatown. Tan had always warned her to be careful walking alone at night, but she had laughed it off, saying he was being paranoid. Now, every time he closes his eyes, he hears the sound of footsteps, the rustling of fabric, and Linh's terrified cry for help. The memories come in disconnected pieces – a flash of her face, contorted in fear; the feel of his phone vibrating with an unknown number; the taste of bile in his mouth as he rushed to the hospital. Tan tries to distract himself by overeating. He tells himself it's just comfort food, but deep down, he knows it's more than that. It's a way to fill the emptiness he feels every time he thinks about Linh. He's gained 20 pounds since her death, and his colleagues have started to notice. They tease him good-naturedly about his love of banh mi sandwiches, but Tan just smiles and says he's stress-eating. As a public defender, Tan is used to dealing with trauma, but nothing could have prepared him for this. He avoids watching TV or reading the news, afraid of triggering another flashback or panic attack. His clients start to notice his distraction, and his performance in court begins to suffer. His boss calls him into her office, concerned about his workload, and Tan breaks down, confessing that he can't shake the feeling of responsibility for Linh's death. At home, Tan becomes obsessed with checking the locks on their apartment door. He does it every time he leaves or enters the building, sometimes even when he's already inside. It's a ritual that brings him temporary comfort, but also serves as a reminder of his failure to protect Linh. He starts to react to false alarms – thinking he hears someone breaking in, only to realize it's just the neighbor's cat meowing. His friends and family try to reassure him, but Tan is certain that danger lurks around every corner. As the months go by, Tan becomes increasingly isolated. He stops attending community events, afraid of running into people who might remind him of Linh. He starts to feel like he's losing himself in grief, and his work begins to suffer as a result. His clients deserve better, and so does he. It's this realization that finally brings Tan to seek help – the hope that therapy can help him find a way to live with his memories, rather than being consumed by them. As he sits in the waiting room, filling out forms and waiting for his appointment, Tan feels a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, he can learn to heal, and find a new sense of purpose without Linh by his side.
